chief_complaint: left lower side abdominal pain and fever for 3 days
hpi_details: 3-day history of constant, aching left lower quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by low-grade fever and chills. Bowel habits have changed to constipation over the past 4 days. No rectal bleeding or melaena. Mild dysuria due to bladder irritation.
ideas: thinks his bowel is twisted or blocked
concerns: afraid he might need emergency bowel surgery or a stoma bag
expectations: wants antibiotics and advice on whether he can eat normally
pmh: diverticulosis diagnosed on screening colonoscopy 3 years ago, essential hypertension
social_hx: ex-smoker (quit 10 years ago), sedentary lifestyle, low-fibre diet

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Diverticulitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Oral or IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or ciprofloxacin/metronidazole depending on severity), liquid/clear fluid diet progressing as pain improves, analgesia (avoid NSAIDs), CT abdomen/pelvis if no improvement in 48 hours or if red flags present, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: left lower side abdominal pain and fever for 3 days

Objective/Exam findings: Check temperature, HR, BP. Abdominal exam for LLQ localized tenderness, localized guarding/rebound. Bloods: FBC, CRP, renal panel. CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast.
Relevant background/PMH: diverticulosis diagnosed on screening colonoscopy 3 years ago, essential hypertension
Current medications: amlodipine 5mg OD, ramipril 10mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Diverticulitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Colorectal carcinoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Signs of peritonitis or a rigid abdomen — would suggest perforation rather than uncomplicated diverticulitis.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 63M with 3-day history of constant, aching left lower quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by low-grade fever and chills. Bowel habits have changed to constipation over the past 4 days. No rectal bleeding or melaena. Mild dysuria due to bladder irritation.
reference_soap.objective: Check temperature, HR, BP. Abdominal exam for LLQ localized tenderness, localized guarding/rebound. Bloods: FBC, CRP, renal panel. CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. DDx: complicated diverticulitis (abscess/perforation), colorectal carcinoma, renal colic, ischaemic colitis.
reference_soap.plan: Oral or IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or ciprofloxacin/metronidazole depending on severity), liquid/clear fluid diet progressing as pain improves, analgesia (avoid NSAIDs), CT abdomen/pelvis if no improvement in 48 hours or if red flags present.

learning_objectives: Recognise the classic presentation of acute diverticulitis in the left lower quadrant
Assess for signs of complications (perforation, peritonitis, abscess, fistula)
Explore dietary habits and bowel regularity
Counsel patient on conservative management vs surgical indications and stoma fears

teaching.one_liner: Small pouches in the colon wall become inflamed or infected, causing steady left-lower-quadrant pain, fever, and a change in bowel habit.
red_flags: Signs of peritonitis or a rigid abdomen — would suggest perforation rather than uncomplicated diverticulitis

must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and is it there all the time or does it come and go?
Have your bowel movements changed — more constipated than usual?
Have you noticed any blood when you go to the toilet?
Have you had a fever or felt shivery?
Does it burn or hurt when you pass urine?
How much fibre do you normally eat, and how active are you day to day?
Has a doctor ever told you that you have diverticulosis?

history.answer: I have had steady pain in the lower left side of my belly and a low fever for the last three days.
The pain started gradually three days ago and built up into a constant ache that hasn't gone away.
It is right down in my lower left abdomen, and it has stayed in that exact spot the whole time.
No, the pain does not spread to my back, my shoulders, or down into my groin.
It is a constant, heavy, dull aching sensation rather than sharp cramps that come and go.
I would rate it around a 6 out of 10, and it has stayed consistently sore since the first day.
Walking around, coughing, or bumping into things makes it throb worse; lying still on my back gives a little relief.
I have had occasional mild twinges down there over the past few years, but never severe, constant pain like this.
I felt slightly nauseous and lost my appetite, but I have not vomited at all.
I have been constipated for four days and haven't passed stool, though I am still passing a small amount of gas.
No, there has been no red blood in my stool, and I haven't noticed any black or tarry stools either.
Yes, I have been running a low-grade fever and shivering with chills on and off for the past three days.
No, my skin and the whites of my eyes look normal, my urine is not dark brown, and my stool has not been pale.
I have noticed a mild burning stinging feeling when I pee since yesterday, but no blood in my urine.
No, I have not felt lightheaded, dizzy, or like I was about to faint.
No chest pressure, chest tightness, or trouble breathing at all.
No, I didn't eat any unusually greasy foods before this started, and I haven't had any heavy alcohol.
I took two paracetamol tablets yesterday which slightly took the edge off, but I have not taken ibuprofen or aspirin.
No heart conditions, irregular heart rhythms like atrial fibrillation, or blood vessel problems that I know of.
I tend to eat mostly bread, meat, and processed foods; I rarely eat vegetables, fresh fruits, or high-fibre meals.
Three years ago during a routine screening colonoscopy, the doctor told me I had little pouches called diverticula in my bowel.
I am worried my bowel might be twisted, tangled up, or completely blocked.
I am really scared that I might need emergency surgery or have to wake up with a stoma bag.
I am hoping you can prescribe antibiotics to clear this infection and let me know whether it is safe for me to eat.
I have high blood pressure, and I was diagnosed with diverticulosis three years ago.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take amlodipine 5 milligrams and ramipril 10 milligrams once a day every morning for my blood pressure.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I smoked about one pack of cigarettes a day for twenty years, but I quit completely ten years ago.
I only drink a glass of beer or wine occasionally on weekends, maybe once or twice a month.
I am a retired postal clerk living at home with my wife, and I live a fairly quiet, sedentary life.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away in his eighties, with no family history of colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.

exam.finding: The patient appears mildly uncomfortable and lies still to avoid worsening his abdominal pain.
Blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 37.9°C, SpO2 98% on ambient air.
Abdomen is symmetric and non-distended without surgical scars or rash.
Hypoactive bowel sounds heard across all quadrants with no vascular bruits.
Tympanitic to percussion throughout with mild localized discomfort over the left lower abdomen.
Marked localized tenderness and mild involuntary guarding in the left lower quadrant; other quadrants are soft and non-tender.
Localized rebound tenderness present exclusively in the left lower quadrant; no diffuse peritonitis or rigid abdomen.
McBurney point tenderness, Rovsing sign, psoas sign, and obturator sign are all absent.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle percussion of either side.
No perianal lesions; digital rectal examination reveals an empty vault without palpable mass, blood, or significant tenderness.
